title_en: Zhang Meiyun v. Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang — dispute over third-party revocation action
ruling_gist_en: A creditor files a third-party revocation action, alleging that the debtor and an outsider obtained a mediation document through a separate sham lawsuit, and took preservation measures against the debtor's property without actual enforcement, thereby harming the creditor's legitimate rights and interests. Where the people's court finds, after trial, that the separate civil lawsuit filed by the debtor and the outsider constitutes a sham lawsuit, the creditor's claim shall be upheld.
keywords_en: Civil; third-party revocation action; sham lawsuit; first instance; basic people's court; Jiangsu Province; natural person; Civil Procedure Law; elements of a third-party revocation action; determination of sham lawsuit; protection of creditor's rights and interests; support the plaintiff; loan dispute; property preservation; Tian Lifang third-party revocation dispute
full_text_en:
Zhang Meiyun v. Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang — dispute over third-party revocation action

[Ruling Summary]

Where a creditor brings a third-party revocation action, claiming that the debtor and a person not party to the case have obtained a mediation paper through a separate false lawsuit, taken preservation measures against the debtor's property but not actually enforced it, thereby harming the creditor's legitimate rights and interests, and if after trial the people's court finds that the civil action separately filed by the debtor and the person not party to the case constitutes a false lawsuit, the creditor's claims shall be supported.

Plaintiff: Zhang Meiyun, female, 67 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Zhu Zhongmin, male, 51 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Tian Lifang, female, 54 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province.

The plaintiff, Zhang Meiyun, filed an action with the Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province, against the defendants, Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang, concerning a dispute over a third-party revocation action.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The plaintiff alleged that during the proceedings of a loan dispute case between the plaintiff and the defendant Tian Lifang, the plaintiff applied for property preservation, and the Yunlong District Court sealed up one house located at No. 7 Wudongzhuang in this city, which was under the name of Tian Lifang. After the case entered the enforcement stage, the plaintiff applied for the evaluation and auction of the sealed-up property of the judgment debtor, Tian Lifang. However, the court informed the plaintiff that the property was subject to a sequential seal-up, and the applicant for the first-priority seal-up was the defendant Zhu Zhongmin. The property did not meet the conditions for auction and the enforcement needed to be suspended. Thereafter, the plaintiff learned that the loan dispute case between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang had been concluded by mediation in the Yunlong District People's Court, and the effective mediation paper confirmed that Tian Lifang owed Zhu Zhongmin a loan of RMB 200,000 plus interest. Based on facts such as Tian Lifang being evasive and stammering when explaining the loan process to the enforcement officers, unable to clarify the context, and fleeing the scene; the contradictions between the IOU she issued to Zhu Zhongmin and her statements to the enforcement authorities; and Zhu Zhongmin's delay in applying to the court for enforcement of the sealed-up property after the mediation paper became effective, the plaintiff had reason to believe that the loan facts between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang were false. The litigation conduct between the two defendants was suspected of being a false lawsuit and seriously harmed the plaintiff's legitimate rights and interests. Therefore, the plaintiff brought this action, requesting the revocation of the Civil Mediation Paper No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 rendered by the Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou City.

Defendant Zhu Zhongmin's Defense: The defendant argued that the loan between himself and the defendant Tian Lifang was objectively true, supported by sufficient evidence, and the evidence had been submitted to the court during the trial of Case No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253. The plaintiff Zhang Meiyun's claims had no factual or legal basis and should be dismissed.

Defendant Tian Lifang's Defense: The defendant argued that during the conversation with the enforcement judge, the judge asked her to leave first to avoid a dispute with the plaintiff Zhang Meiyun, which was not the "fleeing the scene" that the plaintiff claimed. The loan between herself and the defendant Zhu Zhongmin was true, and there were relevant loan receipts to prove it. If it were false, she would be willing to bear all legal liability.

Facts Found by the Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou City at First Instance:

On May 6, 2014, the plaintiff Zhang Meiyun filed an action requesting the defendants Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin to repay the principal and interest of a loan totaling RMB 299,621. The case number was (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 1569. On July 7 of the same year, the defendant Zhu Zhongmin also filed an action requesting Tian Lifang to repay a loan of RMB 200,000 plus interest. The case number was (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253. After the case was filed, Zhu Zhongmin applied for property preservation on July 9, requesting the sealing-up of two properties registered under Tian Lifang's name: No. 7 Dongwuzhuang in this city and Room 203, Building 43-2, Shangdong Garden. The court rendered on the same day the Civil Ruling No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253, ruling to seal up one house located at No. 7 Dongwuzhuang in this city and the property at Room 303, Building 43-2, Shangdong Garden, Hanyuan Avenue, Economic Development Zone, this city. On July 16, 2014, the court served the Civil Ruling No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 and the Notice of Assistance in Enforcement on the Xuzhou Property Registration Office, the assisting enforcement unit. The Xuzhou Property Registration Office fulfilled its assistance obligation. On July 23, 2014, Zhang Meiyun also applied to the court for property preservation: requesting the freezing of the bank deposits of Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin in the amount of RMB 299,621 or the sealing-up or seizure of other property of equivalent value. The court rendered on the same day the Civil Ruling No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 1569, ruling to freeze the bank deposits of the defendants Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin in the amount of RMB 299,621 or to seal up or seize other property of equal value, and served the ruling and the Notice of Assistance in Enforcement to the Xuzhou Real Estate Management Office on the day following the ruling. The Xuzhou Real Estate Management Office also fulfilled its assistance obligation for the seal-up. With respect to the loan dispute between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang, the court mediated the case, and the parties reached a mediation agreement on July 17, 2014. The content of the agreement was: Tian Lifang voluntarily repaid in a lump sum the loan of RMB 200,000 and interest to Zhu Zhongmin before September 30, 2014 (based on RMB 200,000, calculated from June 1, 2013, to the date of payment, at a monthly interest rate of 2%); if Tian Lifang failed to perform the repayment obligation by the due date, interest would continue to be calculated at a monthly interest rate of 2% until the full repayment. The court rendered on the same day the Civil Mediation Paper No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 based on the agreement of both parties and served it on them. After the case was concluded by mediation, although Tian Lifang did not fully perform the repayment obligation as agreed in the mediation agreement, she repaid part of the loan in installments. Therefore, Zhu Zhongmin did not apply for compulsory enforcement in court for a short period and only applied for compulsory enforcement on November 9, 2015. With respect to the loan dispute between Zhang Meiyun and Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin, the court rendered on July 31, 2014, the Civil Judgment No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 1569, after trial, ordering Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin to pay Zhang Meiyun the loan principal and interest totaling RMB 295,525 within five days from the effective date of the judgment and to bear the litigation and preservation costs of RMB 4,920. After the judgment became effective, Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin did not perform the repayment obligation. Zhang Meiyun then applied for compulsory enforcement on August 26, 2014. During the enforcement of this case, Zhang Meiyun learned that Zhu Zhongmin had already applied for the sealing-up of Tian Lifang's property first, and that Zhu Zhongmin, despite Tian Lifang not having performed her repayment obligation to him, neither requested the lifting of the seal-up on the property nor applied to the court for compulsory enforcement. This caused Zhang Meiyun to doubt the authenticity of the loan relationship between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang. In addition, based on the relevant circumstances of Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang that she had learned, Zhang Meiyun believed that Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang had colluded with each other, fabricated a debt, and sought to evade court enforcement through a false lawsuit. Thereafter, Zhang Meiyun filed a revocation action with the court.

Additional Facts Found: In Case No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253, the evidence Zhu Zhongmin used to claim the debt against Tian Lifang consisted of two IOUs, each for a loan amount of RMB 100,000, dated March 18, 2010, and May 11, 2012, respectively. The borrower on the first IOU was Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin, and the other IOU was solely under Tian Lifang's name. The content of both IOUs, including the signature of Tong Taiyin, was written by Tian Lifang. For the first loan of RMB 100,000, both Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang stated that Zhu Zhongmin had withdrawn cash from his account at the Agricultural Bank of China and delivered it; the second loan was delivered by Zhu Zhongmin via bank transfer. During the trial of Case No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253, Zhu Zhongmin submitted a copy of the transaction detail list showing a withdrawal of RMB 100,000 from Jiangsu Bank on March 18, 2010, and the original bank card transaction receipt showing a transfer of RMB 100,000 to Tian Lifang from the Agricultural Bank of China on May 11, 2012. During the trial of this case, the court went to the Hubushan Sub-branch and Minfuyuan Sub-branch of the Agricultural Bank of China and the Chengdong Sub-branch of Jiangsu Bank to obtain the transaction detail lists of withdrawals, transfers, and deposits from the relevant accounts of Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang. These bank transaction detail lists confirmed the authenticity of the evidence submitted by Zhu Zhongmin, and no records of round-trip transactions of the same amount between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang were found.

The above facts are confirmed by the statements of both parties, the case files of Case No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 1569 and Case No. 2253, and the bank card transaction detail lists of Zhu Zhongmin at the Hubushan Sub-branch and Minfuyuan Sub-branch of the Agricultural Bank of China and Tian Lifang at the Chengdong Sub-branch of Jiangsu Bank, which were obtained by the court. The court confirms these facts.

Opinion of the Court at First Instance (Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou City):

According to the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China on third-party revocation actions, a third party bringing a revocation action must provide evidence proving that there is an error in part or in whole in the legally effective judgment, ruling, or mediation paper, and that such error has harmed the third party's civil rights and interests. Otherwise, the claim is not sustainable and shall not be supported. In this case, the authenticity of the loan conduct between the defendant Zhu Zhongmin and the defendant Tian Lifang is proven by the IOUs and the relevant bank transfer and withdrawal receipts. During the trial of this case, the court further investigated the relevant bank accounts of Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang, ex officio and upon the application of the plaintiff Zhang Meiyun, and the investigation results confirmed the facts that Zhu Zhongmin transferred RMB 100,000 to Tian Lifang and withdrew RMB 100,000 from the bank, and no records of Tian Lifang repaying the loan to Zhu Zhongmin were found. In addition, after the mediation paper in Case No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 became effective, it was not contrary to common sense for Zhu Zhongmin not to promptly apply for compulsory enforcement because Tian Lifang had repaid part of the loan; although the case between him and Tian Lifang was filed later than the plaintiff's case, his application for preservation was made before the plaintiff's, and the court's preservation measures in that case were also taken earlier than those in the case between the plaintiff and Tian Lifang. Therefore, it was natural that Zhu Zhongmin's seal-up priority was ahead of the plaintiff's. In summary, the plaintiff's claim that she should have been the first in the seal-up priority of the involved property and that Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang colluded to fabricate the loan facts and engage in a false lawsuit to evade debts and court enforcement is not supported by evidence. Given this premise, the court does not support the plaintiff's request to revoke the Civil Mediation Paper No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 based on subjective suspicion and erroneous judgment of certain facts.

Accordingly, the Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province, rendered a judgment on July 18, 2016, pursuant to Articles 56 and 64 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China:

Judgment: Dismiss the plaintiff Zhang Meiyun's claims.

Zhang Meiyun, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Intermediate People's Court of Xuzhou City, stating: The loan relationship between the appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang was fabricated and harmed the appellant's legitimate rights and interests. The fact that the bank receipts provided by Zhu Zhongmin to the court were false indicated that there was a malicious lawsuit between the appellees. Furthermore, based on the time records of the two withdrawals of Zhu Zhongmin's loan as obtained by the first-instance court, the bank records showed deposits and withdrawals on the same day, which was obviously contrary to common sense. This could lead to the inference that the two IOUs of the appellee Tian Lifang were made afterwards. Obviously, there was no loan relationship between the appellees. In addition, when the appellant sealed up Tian Lifang's property, the real estate department confirmed that the appellant was the first-priority seal-up, but when it came to the auction, it became the second-priority seal-up. How did the appellee Zhu Zhongmin become the first-priority seal-up? Based on the above facts, the appellant requested the court of second instance to investigate the facts in accordance with the law and requested: 1. Revoke the erroneous judgment of the first-instance court in accordance with the law. 2. Revoke the Civil Mediation Paper No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 in accordance with the law. 3. Order the appellees to bear all costs of the appeal.

The appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang argued: 1. The appellant Zhang Meiyun's appeal requests had no factual or legal basis. The appellees requested the court of second instance to dismiss Zhang Meiyun's appeal and affirm the original judgment. 2. The loan between the appellee Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang was objectively true, supported by IOUs and withdrawal and transfer receipts (in the case file). These evidences were original evidence and direct evidence, and could all serve as the basis for deciding the case. 3. The seal-up was based on the ruling and was legally valid. In summary, the appellees requested that Zhang Meiyun's appeal be dismissed and the original judgment be affirmed.

During the second instance proceedings at the Intermediate People's Court of Xuzhou City, the parties submitted evidence in accordance with the law regarding their appeal requests. The court ex officio obtained relevant evidence and organized the parties for evidence exchange and cross-examination.

1. Regarding whether there was a debt of RMB 200,000 principal between the appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang, the appellant Zhang Meiyun argued during the second instance that the IOUs dated March 18, 2010, and May 11, 2012, written by Tian Lifang, which were used in the original case (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 to prove the existence of the RMB 200,000 loan principal between the appellees, were false. Zhang Meiyun applied to the court for forensic examination. The Judicial Authentication Science and Technology Research Institute issued an opinion stating that it was impossible to determine the specific formation time of the March 18, 2010 IOU, but the five fingerprints at the "2012" place, the "2013" place, the left side "Tian Lifang" place, the "May" place, and the lower right "Tian Lifang" place on the IOU were formed by a single simultaneous impression, not formed on the respective indicated dates; it was impossible to determine the specific formation time of the May 11, 2012 IOU and the formation time of the fingerprints on it. Regarding this, the appellant argued that both IOUs were false. The appellees argued that the specific formation time of the IOUs should be examined, and the time of fingerprint impression did not prove anything. However, before and after the cross-examination of this authentication opinion, the appellees gave inconsistent statements as to how the two IOUs were formed. Zhu Zhongmin submitted to the court a receipt showing a withdrawal of RMB 100,000 from his account No. 622866110011XXXX at Jiangsu Bank on March 18, 2010, as evidence that the loan had been delivered. Zhang Meiyun argued that this evidence was false.

2. Regarding how the appellee Tian Lifang repaid the loan to the appellee Zhu Zhongmin after the loan occurred, the appellees gave inconsistent statements. Pursuant to Article 64, Paragraph 2 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court ex officio obtained the bank account transactions between the appellees from May 11, 2012 to May 11, 2013, which showed that Tian Lifang had made four repayments of RMB 6,000 each via bank transfer on December 27, 2012, February 7, 2013, March 31, 2013, and May 11, 2013. The appellant argued that there were other economic transactions between the appellees. The appellees argued that the repayments were real.

3. Regarding how the appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang repaid the loan after reaching the mediation agreement, the appellees were unclear about the form of repayment and the specific items of repayment and did not provide relevant transfer evidence to support their claims. The appellant Zhang Meiyun argued that this repayment was false and that in all previous trials, the appellees had never mentioned how they repaid each other.

4. Regarding why the appellee Zhu Zhongmin only applied for enforcement of RMB 95,000 against the appellee Tian Lifang, Zhu Zhongmin stated that after reaching the mediation in Case No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253, Tian Lifang had already repaid RMB 200,000, and the enforcement target of RMB 95,000 was an approximate calculation. Tian Lifang confirmed Zhu Zhongmin's statement. The appellant Zhang Meiyun denied this and argued that it was a false lawsuit.

5. Regarding whether the appellant Zhang Meiyun had standing to bring this action, the appellee Zhu Zhongmin provided the court with the Civil Ruling No. (2014) Yun Min Che Chu Zi No. 0005, which showed that the appellant had previously filed a revocation action and then withdrew it, and that her new revocation action had exceeded the statutory time limit and should not be permitted. Zhang Meiyun argued that the withdrawal of the action in (2014) Yun Min Che Chu Zi No. 0005 was not her true intent.

Regarding the facts disputed by the parties, the Intermediate People's Court of Xuzhou City found as follows: On March 18, 2010, the appellee Tian Lifang issued an IOU to the appellee Zhu Zhongmin for RMB 100,000, indicating the borrowers as Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin. It stipulated a monthly interest rate of 2%, with interest of RMB 6,000 payable every three months, a term of one year, and a penalty of RMB 30,000 for late repayment in addition to the agreed interest. Subsequently, Tian Lifang modified the "10" to "12" on the IOU. Thereafter, Tian Lifang wrote on the IOU "March 18, 2013, Tian Lifang" and "May 18, 2014, Tian Lifang". Tian Lifang placed her fingerprints at the aforementioned dates and signature locations. On May 11, 2012, Tian Lifang issued another IOU to Zhu Zhongmin for RMB 100,000, stipulating a monthly interest rate of 2%. In Zhu Zhongmin's complaint in Case No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253, it was stated: "The defendant (Tian Lifang) urgently needed funds for business and borrowed RMB 200,000 from the plaintiff (Zhu Zhongmin) on two occasions with interest agreed upon. However, the defendant broke her promise, leaving the plaintiff no choice but to file this lawsuit. The plaintiff requests the court to order the repayment of the loan of RMB 200,000 and interest, with the litigation costs borne by the defendant." In the trial of that case, Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang did not address the performance of the loan agreement, including repayment.

Additional Facts Found: Because the appellee Tian Lifang failed to perform the obligations determined in Civil Judgment No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 1569, the appellant Zhang Meiyun applied to the first-instance court for compulsory enforcement against Tian Lifang and Tong Taiyin, with an enforcement target of RMB 300,445. The first-instance court, finding no property available for enforcement against the judgment debtor, concluded the enforcement of the current instance by enforcement ruling No. (2014) Yun Zhi Zi No. 1470 on November 6, 2015. Tian Lifang did not perform her obligations under the Civil Mediation Paper No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253. The appellee Zhu Zhongmin applied for enforcement to the first-instance court on November 9, 2015, with an enforcement target of RMB 95,000. During the enforcement process, Zhu Zhongmin stated to the first-instance court on May 6, 2016, that Tian Lifang had an intention to repay, and the applicant temporarily did not request the auction of the judgment debtor's property. This case was concluded on May 6, 2016, due to the inability to close the case despite exhausting enforcement measures, by enforcement ruling No. (2015) Yun Zhi Zi No. 2314, concluding the current enforcement procedure.

Further Facts Found: The appellant Zhang Meiyun had previously filed a revocation action with the first-instance court against the appellees Tian Lifang and Zhu Zhongmin on November 14, 2014, and later withdrew the action on December 17, 2014. The first-instance court rendered Civil Ruling No. (2014) Yun Min Che Chu Zi No. 0005 on December 17, 2014, permitting Zhang Meiyun to withdraw the action.

Other facts of the second instance are consistent with the facts found at first instance.

The Intermediate People's Court of Xuzhou City held that the issues in dispute in the second instance were: 1. Whether the appellant Zhang Meiyun had standing to bring this revocation action; 2. Whether the appellant's exercise of the right to bring a revocation action exceeded the statutory time limit; 3. Whether the debtor-creditor relationship involving a loan principal of RMB 200,000 and interest between the appellee Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang actually existed; 4. Whether the Civil Mediation Paper No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 reached between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang involved a false lawsuit; 5. Whether Zhang Meiyun's legitimate rights and interests were harmed by the Civil Mediation Paper No. (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253.

1. The Appellant Zhang Meiyun is a qualified litigant in this case. The Appellant claims that she did not participate in the (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 litigation between the Appellees, and that the mediation agreement reached between the Appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang in that case involved false litigation. The debt of RMB 200,000 principal and interest owed by Tian Lifang to Zhu Zhongmin is a fictitious debt. Zhu Zhongmin first preserved Tian Lifang's real property but did not apply for compulsory execution, thereby obstructing the realization of the Appellant's claims against Tian Lifang. Pursuant to Article 292 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the Appellant should be recognized as a qualified plaintiff in this third-party action to set aside the judgment.

2. The Appellant Zhang Meiyun's exercise of the third-party action to set aside the judgment did not exceed the statutory time limit. Pursuant to Article 292 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, a third party who brings an action to set aside a legally effective judgment, ruling, or mediation document shall file the action with the people's court that rendered the effective judgment, ruling, or mediation document within six months from the date on which it knew or should have known that its civil rights and interests were harmed. After the Appellant applied for enforcement against the Appellee Tian Lifang on August 26, 2014, she only then learned that the Appellee Zhu Zhongmin had obtained the (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 civil mediation agreement before she had an enforcement title, and that Zhu Zhongmin had taken preservation measures against Tian Lifang's property before she did. Subsequently, on November 14, 2014, she filed a third-party action to set aside the judgment with the court of first instance. Therefore, the Appellant should be recognized as having asserted her rights within the statutory period. Although the Appellant withdrew the lawsuit on December 17, 2014, pursuant to Article 214 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, it is lawful for the Appellant to file a third-party action to set aside the judgment again after withdrawal.

3. The creditor-debtor relationship between the Appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang regarding the principal of RMB 200,000 and its interest in the original case cannot be recognized as complete and genuinely existing.

(1) The IOU for the principal loan of RMB 100,000 dated March 18, 2010, which was provided by the Appellee Zhu Zhongmin as the creditor to the court of first instance in the original case, has defects. Evidence must be genuine and free from defects to have formal probative value under procedural law; only then can the court examine and determine the substantive probative value, such as whether the content of the evidence is relevant to the facts to be proved. In the IOU dated March 18, 2010, the signature section contains multiple notations of different dates, signatures, and fingerprints, differing from common IOUs. The Appellee Tian Lifang, as the issuer of the IOU, stated that it was written at the request of the creditor Zhu Zhongmin to prove "continued use." Before the cross-examination of the expert opinion, Tian Lifang claimed that the dates and fingerprints on the IOU were "applied one at a time." Zhu Zhongmin, as the holder of the IOU, made a similar statement to Tian Lifang regarding the formation of the signatures, dates, and fingerprints on the IOU, expressly stating that the modification from "10" to "12" was "the fingerprint applied at that time," but was unclear about other details. After the expert opinion concluded that "the fingerprints in the signature section of the IOU were formed at one time," Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang changed their previous statements, asserting that "the key issue is the time the IOU was created and the time the fingerprints were applied cannot deny the authenticity of the loan." Although the expert opinion did not conclude the specific formation of the IOU, it reached a clear conclusion regarding the formation of most fingerprints on the IOU. The Appellees objected to the expert opinion but did not present circumstances meeting the requirements of Article 27 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, nor did they provide counter-evidence to prove the expert opinion was false. Therefore, the conclusion of the expert opinion should be adopted. Since the Appellees are the holder and issuer of the IOU respectively, and they could not provide a reasonable explanation for its formation, the IOU dated March 18, 2010, is deemed defective and cannot serve as the basis for deciding the case.

(2) The performance action brought by the Appellee Zhu Zhongmin as the creditor in the original case lacked clear performance circumstances by the debtor Tian Lifang. According to the agreements in the IOUs dated March 18, 2010, and May 11, 2012, Tian Lifang should pay interest and liquidated damages to Zhu Zhongmin. However, Zhu Zhongmin claimed the loan was RMB 200,000, yet the Appellees, as lender and borrower, provided vague descriptions of key matters regarding the existence of the creditor-debtor relationship, such as how the loan principal, interest, and liquidated damages were to be repaid. Neither Zhu Zhongmin's statement in the complaint nor the statements of Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang in the original case described how Tian Lifang, as the debtor, performed the obligations after the loan was made. Furthermore, Zhu Zhongmin's claims in the original case only mentioned the loan of RMB 200,000 without specifying the specific amount of interest or the method of calculation, claiming that "the interest could not be calculated, so interest was not calculated," which is incomprehensible to an ordinary person.

(3) There were contradictions among the evidence in the original case. The mediation in the original case was based on the IOUs, bank transaction records and receipts, and the complaint. The bank transaction records and receipts could only prove the possibility of delivery of the RMB 200,000 loan and the establishment of the creditor-debtor relationship, but could not prove the final status of that relationship. However, the IOUs explicitly provided for interest and liquidated damages, which clearly contradicted the complaint. Pursuant to Article 63(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the statements of the parties are a form of evidence. The statements of the Appellees in the original case, which lacked facts regarding repayment, contradicted the IOU as a documentary piece of evidence. The mediation in the original case did not comply with Article 93 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC.

In summary, it cannot be concluded solely based on the facts that the Appellee Zhu Zhongmin withdrew RMB 100,000 on March 18, 2010, and transferred RMB 100,000 to the Appellee Tian Lifang on May 11, 2012, along with the IOUs and Tian Lifang's admission, that a complete and detailed creditor-debtor relationship of RMB 200,000 in principal and interest existed between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang.

4. The Appellee Zhu Zhongmin made false statements in the original case, and the Appellee Tian Lifang made a false admission. Therefore, the litigation in the original case between the Appellees should be found to be false litigation. Pursuant to Article 13(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, civil litigation shall adhere to the principle of good faith. Litigants have a duty of good faith, which requires that during civil proceedings, they shall not intentionally make false statements contrary to their subjective knowledge of the truth; it does not mean they have an obligation to make statements based on objective truth.

(1) The Appellee Zhu Zhongmin made false statements in the original case. As the creditor, Zhu Zhongmin gave inconsistent statements regarding issues such as how the loan was repaid, whether the repayment included interest, how interest was paid, and the period of payment. In the proceedings of this case, he repeatedly explained his inconsistent statements as "I don't remember," "I'm not clear," "it's been a long time, I forgot," etc. After the mediation in the original case, the Appellant Zhang Meiyun immediately raised objections to the original case and persistently raised objections to the court of first instance and the opposing party over many years. Zhu Zhongmin merely excused himself with simple "I don't remember" or "I'm not clear" without providing substantial reasons, which is not convincing to an ordinary person. In particular, after the court presented the mediation agreement of the original case, the expert opinion, and the bank account transactions between Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang investigated by the court ex officio—which were sufficient to refute his previous statements—Zhu Zhongmin changed his answers to the aforementioned issues without providing substantial reasons or evidence to explain why he had made inconsistent statements. His statements cannot be deemed truthful. Since Zhu Zhongmin's statements regarding his personal experience—such as the formation of the IOUs and the method and timing of interest payments—conflict with confirmed documentary evidence and the expert opinion, it should be found that Zhu Zhongmin made false statements in both the original case and this case.

(2) The Appellee Tian Lifang made a false admission in the original case. As the debtor, Tian Lifang lacked a defense in the original case. She made no statements on matters closely related to her own interests, such as whether repayment occurred, the start and end dates of repayment, or the specific methods of repayment, only stating that she had no objection to the creditor Zhu Zhongmin's claims. Moreover, between Tian Lifang and Zhu Zhongmin, there was not only cash repayment admitted by Tian Lifang in the second instance but also repayments through bank accounts, with the repayment period extending beyond what Tian Lifang claimed. A party's intentional admission of the other party's false claims does not bind the court. The mediation in the original case, which was based on Tian Lifang's admission, was inappropriate.

(3) There was collusion between the Appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang. The Appellees not only gave inconsistent statements regarding how the loan was repaid and how the mediation agreement was performed after it was reached, but also their statements contradicted each other. On one hand, the Appellees argued in the second instance of this case that only cash repayments existed. On the other hand, they jointly failed to provide the court with evidence of multiple repayments made through their bank accounts. This conduct cannot be excused as simple forgetfulness and should be found as concealment of evidence. After the court presented partial bank transaction records between the Appellees, the expert opinion, and the mediation agreement of the original case, they simultaneously changed their previous statements to form consistent statements. This change of statements should be found as collusion. Furthermore, after the mediation agreement was reached, regarding how the RMB 200,000 was repaid and the scope of repayment, Zhu Zhongmin claimed that in August 2014, Tian Lifang repaid RMB 200,000 in two installments, which included interest, litigation fees, preservation fees, and part of the principal. Tian Lifang had no understanding of the specific items of repayment and initially gave vague statements about the repayment facts, only confirming them after Zhu Zhongmin specified the repayment time. Tian Lifang first claimed to have transferred two installments of RMB 100,000 each at a bank counter using the bank card of a third party, Miao Long. When the court requested the bank forms she filled out, she changed her statement to claim that the transfer was made through an ATM. However, she was unable to provide evidence that she had obtained bank authorization to transfer amounts exceeding the ATM's RMB 50,000 upper limit. Therefore, the fact that the RMB 200,000 had been repaid cannot be confirmed.

5. The Appellant Zhang Meiyun's claims were harmed by the conduct of the Appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang in the original case, as she was unable to obtain proper satisfaction.

(1) The Appellee Zhu Zhongmin, as an enforcement applicant, first took preservation measures and then delayed applying for compulsory execution, affecting the enforcement of the Appellant Zhang Meiyun's case against the creditor. After Zhu Zhongmin preserved Tian Lifang's property, a mediation agreement was reached on July 17, 2014, which stipulated that Tian Lifang voluntarily repay Zhu Zhongmin the RMB 200,000 loan and interest in a lump sum by September 30, 2014 (with the principal of RMB 200,000 as the base, interest calculated from June 1, 2013, to the date of repayment at a monthly rate of 2%); if Tian Lifang failed to perform the repayment obligation when due, interest would continue to be calculated at a monthly rate of 2% until the loan is fully repaid. After the performance period expired, Zhu Zhongmin did not apply for compulsory execution until November 9, 2015. Zhang Meiyun, as a creditor, applied for compulsory execution to the court of first instance on August 26, 2014, but her application was frustrated by Zhu Zhongmin's prior preservation measures.

(2) The Appellee Zhu Zhongmin adopted a high preservation amount but a low enforcement application target, and failed to apply for a change in the preservation method, thereby affecting the realization of the Appellant Zhang Meiyun's claims. Zhu Zhongmin preserved two properties of Tian Lifang with a preservation target of RMB 280,000. Tian Lifang held a 40% share in each of the preserved properties. Zhu Zhongmin, using the (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 civil mediation document as the enforcement title, applied for enforcement of only RMB 95,000. On one hand, Zhu Zhongmin claimed that the RMB 95,000 was an approximate figure; on the other hand, he neither applied for an appraisal and auction of the preserved properties nor applied for a change in the subject matter of enforcement, thereby affecting Zhang Meiyun's enforcement against Tian Lifang. Therefore, it should be found that the (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 civil mediation document infringed upon Zhang Meiyun's lawful rights and interests.

6. The Appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang engaged in malicious collusion in the mediation of the original case and in the first- and second-instance proceedings of this case by providing defective evidence, concealing relevant evidence, and making false statements. Such conduct should be punished. In the (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 case and the first instance of this case, Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang repeatedly altered the dates in the IOU of March 18, 2010, applied fingerprints multiple times while falsely claiming the authenticity of the IOU, concealed the bank transfers of loan repayments between them, falsely claimed part of the facts regarding repayment of principal and interest, and through preservation measures, first seized the property and then failed to apply for enforcement of the preserved subject matter, thereby obstructing the realization of the rights of the obligee. They used these actions to defend themselves in the mediation of the original case and in the first- and second-instance proceedings of this case, misleading the judges in different proceedings, delaying the case for several years, obstructing the realization of the obligee's rights, and causing the Appellant to continuously petition. The court shall issue a separate decision to impose sanctions on the Appellees' unlawful litigation conduct.

7. The court of the original case, based on the deceptive conduct of the Appellees Zhu Zhongmin and Tian Lifang in the original case, rendered the (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 civil mediation document, which harmed judicial credibility. The People's Court of Yunlong District, Xuzhou City, based on the litigation materials provided by the Appellees, fell into erroneous judgment and formed a mistaken inner conviction. The (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 civil mediation document it issued led Zhu Zhongmin to create a claim through preservation of Tian Lifang's properties without applying for compulsory execution of the preserved properties, thereby obstructing the realization of the Appellant Zhang Meiyun's claims against Tian Lifang and harming judicial credibility. Pursuant to Article 10 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning the Handling of Economic Dispute Cases Involving Economic Crimes and Article 12 of the Guiding Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Preventing and Sanctioning False Litigation, the clues and materials relating to criminal suspicion in this case shall be transferred to the relevant public security organs and procuratorial authorities for investigation and handling.

In summary, the original judgment was based on unclear factual findings and erroneous application of the law. The Appellant Zhang Meiyun's appeal claims are established. The original mediation document involved false litigation, infringing upon the Appellant's interests, and should be reversed in accordance with the law. Accordingly, the Intermediate People's Court of Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province, pursuant to Article 55(2) and Article 58(1)(4) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, Articles 112 and 170(1)(2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, and Articles 190(2), 292, and 300(1)(1) of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rendered the following judgment on August 2, 2017:

I. Set aside the civil judgment (2016) Su 0303 Min Che No. 1 of the People's Court of Yunlong District, Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province;

II. Set aside the civil mediation document (2014) Yun Min Chu Zi No. 2253 of the People's Court of Yunlong District, Xuzhou City, Jiangsu Province;

III. Dismiss the claims of the Appellee Zhu Zhongmin against the Appellee Tian Lifang for repayment of the loan principal of RMB 200,000 and interest.

The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 2,300 and the appraisal fee of RMB 6,600 shall be borne by the Appellee Zhu Zhongmin.

This judgment is final.
